# Models

<!-- Generated by scripts/describe_models.py from config/ and src/; do not edit by hand. -->

Every model the two builds read, with every parameter it is fitted with: the config's own
values and, marked *default*, the wrapper's defaults underneath them. How the members are
combined (NNLS stack, Rome layer, overrides, cell shift, bounds) is in the
[README](../README.md#how-it-works).

- **Final submission**: [`hp_cb03_it4500`](#hp_cb03_it4500), [`hp_cb04_it4500`](#hp_cb04_it4500), [`q04s_q04_snow`](#q04s_q04_snow), [`ab07s_ab07_snow`](#ab07s_ab07_snow), [`rb01s_rb01_snow`](#rb01s_rb01_snow), [`f25s_f25_snow`](#f25s_f25_snow); also fitted, with NNLS weight 0 everywhere: [`t05s_t05_snow`](#t05s_t05_snow); Rome layer [`r14_rules_plus_unmatched_route`](#r14_rules_plus_unmatched_route), [`lg01_lirf_gate_delay`](#lg01_lirf_gate_delay); [`ab07_ab02_adsb_calib`](#ab07_ab02_adsb_calib) for the Rome matched-row blend.
- **v62**: [`t05_huber_alpha[alpha=600]`](#t05_huber_alphaalpha600), [`f25_queue2`](#f25_queue2), [`q04_c12_min_leaf30`](#q04_c12_min_leaf30), [`rb01_lirf_route_ab02`](#rb01_lirf_route_ab02), [`ab07_ab02_adsb_calib`](#ab07_ab02_adsb_calib), [`cb03_k20_combo_adsb`](#cb03_k20_combo_adsb), [`cb04_cb03_adsb_calib`](#cb04_cb03_adsb_calib); the same Rome layer.

Seeds are fixed (LightGBM `seed` 0, CatBoost `random_seed` 0). The final phase's refits
run under the `laptop` machine profile, which sets LightGBM's `num_threads` = 4, `verbosity` = -1 (the defaults); LightGBM's result can change in the last digits with the thread count.

## Fold sets

| fold set | folds (held-out months; each trains on the other months of 2025) |
|---|---|
| `final_pairs` | 2025-01_2025-07: 01, 07; 2025-02_2025-06: 02, 06 |
| `seasonal` | 2025-01: 01; 2025-07: 07 |

Cross-validation predicts each held-out month from a model fitted on the other months;
the refit fits all twelve months of 2025 and predicts the 2026 rows. Target-dependent
blocks are recomputed inside every fold from its training rows only.

## Configs

### `hp_cb03_it4500`

*final submission: stack member.* Config: [`config/experiments/hp_cb03_it4500.yaml`](../config/experiments/hp_cb03_it4500.yaml)

> cb03's recipe with one change: 4,500 iterations instead of 3,000 at the same learning rate --
> the change that moved its sibling cb04 by -1.36 over four months (hp_cb04_it4500; every month
> better) and passed the stack gate (-0.46 against F1).
> Question: does cb03, which also serves the NM-unmatched rows alone, under-fit the same way?
> Baseline: cb03_k20_combo_adsb on final_pairs, same code: trimmed RMSE without Rome 198.20
> (Jan 186.96, Feb 221.47, Jun 172.15, Jul 211.30).
> Population: all departures of the four held-out months. Reading, fixed before running: judged in
> the stack (a129, against F1 with cb04 at 4,500) as a replacement for cb03 and as an addition beside
> it; accepted only if the stack's trimmed RMSE without Rome improves on at least 3 of the 4 months
> and by at least 0.3 s over the four.

| training option | value |
|---|---|
| fold set | `final_pairs` |
| training labels capped at | 10,800 s |
| prediction clip | none |
| target transform | none |
| relabelled training rows | no |

### `r14_rules_plus_unmatched_route`

*both builds: Rome layer.* Config: [`config/experiments/r14_rules_plus_unmatched_route.yaml`](../config/experiments/r14_rules_plus_unmatched_route.yaml)

> The Rome (LIRF) layer: two rules over a LightGBM routed on the NM flight-match flag.
> Rule 1: an NM-unmatched LIRF departure that took off more than 12 h after its schedule gets
> 0.62 x gap + 0.38 x 87,540 s, a mixture of the two values such labels take in 2025 (the gap
> itself, or about one day plus a normal taxi). Rule 2: an NM-matched departure whose
> takeoff - aobt_3 exceeds 4 h gets that difference. Everything else: one LightGBM for
> NM-unmatched rows and one for matched rows, each also trained on the other's rows at weight 0.1.
> Predictions clipped to [300, 200,000] s. CV RMSE on LIRF rows (Jan + Jul 2025): 625.06.

| training option | value |
|---|---|
| fold set | `seasonal` |
| training labels capped at | no cap |
| prediction clip | none |
| target transform | none |
| relabelled training rows | no |

**`rules`**, with these settings:

```yaml
clip:
- 300.0
- 200000.0
rules:
- name: lirf_unmatched_12h
  when:
  - column: flt_no_match
    op: ==
    value: 1
  - column: airport
    op: in
    value:
    - LIRF
  - column: sc_gap_sec
    op: '>'
    value: 43200
  predict:
    mix:
    - weight: 0.62
      column: sc_gap_sec
    - weight: 0.38
      constant: 87540
- name: aobt_identity_extreme
  when:
  - column: flt_no_match
    op: ==
    value: 0
  - column: ob_aobt_sec
    op: '>'
    value: 14400
  predict:
    column: ob_aobt_sec
```

and this inner model:

**`routed`**, with these settings:

```yaml
by: flt_no_match
routes:
  unmatched:
  - 1
foreign_weight: 0.1
min_rows: 3000
```

and this inner model (one per route):

### `lg01_lirf_gate_delay`

*both builds: Rome layer.* Config: [`config/experiments/lg01_lirf_gate_delay.yaml`](../config/experiments/lg01_lirf_gate_delay.yaml)

> Gate-delay model for Rome, after team likable-eagle: taxi-out T = D - G, with D = takeoff - schedule
> (known on the ranking rows) and G the gate delay, which is what is learnt. Fitted on LIRF

## Feature blocks

Kinds: `row_local` reads only the row's own fields; `context` reads other rows but never
a label, and is computed once over training and 2026 rows together; `target_dependent`
reads labels and is recomputed inside every fold from its training rows. Columns named
`cat_*` are categorical.

### adsb

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/adsb.py`](../src/taxiout/features/adsb.py); used by 8 of the 16 configs above.

ADS-B: each departure's own ground segment and takeoff, from adsb.lol traces.

The idea of ADS-B features on every departure, and their shape, come from team outgoing-boat's
public solution, where they were worth −16.2 board seconds
(https://github.com/EnioAguiar/prc-taxiout-2026). The code is ours. The traces are pulled by
`scripts/pull_adsb.py` into
`data/external/adsb/cut/YYYY.MM.DD.parquet` (adsb.lol, ODbL 1.0: "Contains information from
adsb.lol").

**Events.** Points sorted by aircraft (`icao`) and time. A ground point continues the current
ground segment if the previous point is the same aircraft, also on the ground, and less than
`SEG_GAP` s earlier. A segment ends in a **takeoff** when its last ground point is followed,
within `TAKEOFF_GAP` s, by an airborne point of the same aircraft; the takeoff time is that
airborne point's. Per segment: first ground point, first point moving faster than `MOVE_KT`,
the ground speed and position of the first point, point count, largest gap, share of MLAT points.

**Matching** (no aircraft identity exists in the challenge data). Candidates are (a) same airport
and same callsign — `callsign` from the flight record, else `flight_no` — with takeoffs within
`CS_TOL` s, priority 0; (b) same airport, nearest takeoff before and after within `TIME_TOL` s,
priority 1. Assigned greedily by (priority, |Δt|), each departure and each event used once.
Days are processed one at a time with the last two hours of the previous day, so taxis crossing
midnight are seen; an event belongs to the day of its takeoff.

**Features**, NaN where unmatched: `adsb_taxi = mvt − first_ground`, `adsb_taxi_move = mvt −
first_move`, `adsb_gs0`, `adsb_takeoff_err = takeoff − mvt`, `adsb_n_ground`,
`adsb_gap_max`, `adsb_frac_mlat`, `adsb_lat0`, `adsb_lon0`, `adsb_match_pri`. Never
substitute `adsb_taxi` for the prediction: the trace starts late by an airport-specific amount
(outgoing-boat: EHAM +6 s, EGLL −1,076 s); the model learns that.

`CONTEXT`: external data and other rows; never a departure's label. **The cache key does not see
the trace files** (registry docstring): rebuild with `--overwrite` after the pull changes.

Columns: `adsb_taxi`, `adsb_taxi_move`, `adsb_gs0`, `adsb_takeoff_err`, `adsb_n_ground`, `adsb_gap_max`, `adsb_frac_mlat`, `adsb_lat0`, `adsb_lon0`, `adsb_match_pri`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
{SEG_GAP: 600.0, TAKEOFF_GAP: 120.0, MOVE_KT: 1.0, CS_TOL: 300.0, TIME_TOL: 90.0, LOOKBACK: 7200.0}
```

### adsb_calib

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/adsb_calib.py`](../src/taxiout/features/adsb_calib.py); used by 4 of the 16 configs above.

The trace, re-expressed against this airport-month's own receiver behaviour (label-free).

`scripts/analysis/a115_adsb_drift_and_error_budget.py` measured the drift the challenge Discord
warned about: adsb.lol's receivers changed between 2025 and 2026. At EGLL the median of
`adsb_taxi_move − (mvt − aobt_3)` — how much later than the recorded off-block the trace first
shows movement — went from −842 / −1,093 s
(Jan / Jul 2025) to −538 / −244 s (Jan / Jul 2026), while coverage went from 21% / 8% to 60% / 98%.
A model that learnt "an EGLL trace starts ~1,000 s after off-block" from 2025 over-predicts every
traced EGLL row in 2026. Nothing in the 2025 folds can show this.

The remedy is to hand the model the trace **relative to its own month**. Per airport × UTC month,
from that month's departures alone, with no label involved:

* `ad_match_rate_m`: share of departures with a matched trace (the receiver coverage);
* `ad_med_lag_m`: median of `adsb_taxi_move − (mvt − aobt_3)` over traced rows with an AOBT
  (the typical lag of the trace behind the recorded off-block, this month);
* `ad_med_n_ground_m`: median point count of the month's traces (receiver density).

And per departure:

* `ad_taxi_move_adj = adsb_taxi_move − ad_med_lag_m`: the trace-implied taxi with this month's
  typical lag removed — comparable across months and airports;
* `ad_lag_vs_m = (adsb_taxi_move − (mvt − aobt_3)) − ad_med_lag_m`: how unusual this trace's
  start is for the month (a late-starting trace, or an off-block record that disagrees with it);
* `ad_n_ground_rel = adsb_n_ground / ad_med_n_ground_m`: trace density relative to the month.

The statistics use the whole month, including rows after the departure; the organisers state the
model is post-operational and whole-day statistics are already in use (`runway_history`). Reads
the cached `adsb` block (`CONTEXT`; rebuild with `--overwrite` when `adsb` is rebuilt).

Columns: `ad_match_rate_m`, `ad_med_lag_m`, `ad_med_n_ground_m`, `ad_taxi_move_adj`, `ad_lag_vs_m`, `ad_n_ground_rel`.

### arrival_regime

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/arrival_regime.py`](../src/taxiout/features/arrival_regime.py); used by 7 of the 16 configs above.

The day's `block_time` copy regime, read off the arrivals.

A departure's label is exact whenever its `block_time` copies a stamp we hold, and the ranking
set hides `block_time` for departures only — arrival rows keep theirs. On 2025, where both
directions carry labels, the share of an airport-day's arrivals whose on-
block time copies a stamp tracks the share of that day's departures whose off-block time does:
correlation 0.50 across airport-days and **0.33 within airport**. So the arrivals expose, label-
free, a day-level property of how the data provider recorded block times, which the departure
classifier (`modes5`) cannot see — it knows the airport, not the day.

An arrival "copies" when its on-block `block_time` is within `TOL` seconds of `arvt_3`,
`arvt_1`, `sched_time` or its own landing `mvt_time`, first match in that order. 2025 shares:
`sched_time` 5.2%, `arvt_1` 3.9%, `arvt_3` 0.3%, landing 0.03%, none 90.5%.

Whole-day shares are used, as `runway_history` uses whole-day statistics: the organisers state the
model is post-operational, and every input is an arrival row the ranking set carries intact.
`CONTEXT`: other rows, never a departure's label.

Columns: `ar_day_copy`, `ar_day_sched`, `ar_day_arvt1`, `ar_day_n`, `ar_opm_copy`, `ar_opm_n`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
TOL: 60.0
ARR_STAMPS: [arvt_3, arvt_1, sched_time, mvt_time]
```

### calendar

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/calendar.py`](../src/taxiout/features/calendar.py); used by 16 of the 16 configs above.

Calendar and time-of-day features, in each airport's local civil time.

Operations follow the local clock — curfews, banks of departures, night restrictions — so the
local hour matters more than the UTC one, and DST has to be handled rather than approximated
with a fixed offset.

Columns: `cal_local_minute_of_day`, `cal_local_hour`, `cal_dow`, `cal_doy`, `cal_month`, `cal_is_weekend`, `cal_tod_sin`, `cal_tod_cos`.

### congestion

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/congestion.py`](../src/taxiout/features/congestion.py); used by 16 of the 16 configs above.

Traffic around the departure: how busy the airport and the runway were, and for how long.

Early on this looked like the biggest untouched lever, but the evidence was split, and this block
exists to settle it rather than to argue it.

Against: an early review built rolling counts ad hoc and measured them at 0.042 correlation with
a baseline model's residual (0.144 with the target), which is about 0.4 s of RMSE. Its
argument for why is the strong one — `ob_aobt_sec` is Eurocontrol's reconstruction of the
actual off-block time, so on the 98.4% of rows that carry it the queue is already *inside* the
feature the model leans on hardest, and this block can only restate it.

For: a group-mean oracle over `airport x runway x 10 min` has a ceiling near 11.5 s once
corrected for the shrinkage attenuation we measured — the review's own estimate of 1.4 s came
through an estimator that recovers 12% of a
known effect at 3.4 rows per group. That ceiling is for *any* feature resolving the cell exactly,
and counts are a coarse function of it, so the two findings can both be true.

So the columns here are deliberately not all counts. `cg_prev_gap_rw` and `cg_stand_idle_s`
are timings rather than volumes, and the runway-level windows are the ones the 0.318
autocorrelation of taxi-out at a 2-5 minute lag points at.

`CONTEXT`: every input is another row's `mvt_time` or `block_time`, never a departure's
`taxi_sec`. Departure takeoff times and complete arrival records are both present in the
ranking set, so this is computed contemporaneously for 2026 rather than carried over.

Columns: `cg_dep_5m`, `cg_dep_15m`, `cg_dep_60m`, `cg_dep_rw_5m`, `cg_dep_rw_15m`, `cg_arr_15m`, `cg_arr_60m`, `cg_prev_gap_rw`, `cg_stand_idle_s`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
AIRPORT_WINDOWS:
- [5m, 5m]
- [15m, 15m]
- [60m, 60m]
RUNWAY_WINDOWS:
- [5m, 5m]
- [15m, 15m]
```

### consistency

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/consistency.py`](../src/taxiout/features/consistency.py); used by 14 of the 16 configs above.

Whether the record agrees with itself, and which plan value the actual was copied from.

`block_time` is written by a recording system, not measured, and on a large minority of rows it
holds a *plan* value rather than an actual one — the schedule, or one of the Network Manager
estimates. Classified by mode: the A-CDM actual on 38.9% of 2025 departures, the schedule
on a further 5.1% where `aobt_3` says something different, a plan value on 3.3%. Those modes have
very different residuals: 145 s on the A-CDM rows against 750 s on the schedule-copied ones.

The model cannot currently tell them apart. It sees `ob_aobt_sec`, `ob_eobt_sec` and `ob_sched_sec`
as separate continuous columns and would have to *subtract* them to notice that two agree
exactly — which a tree cannot do in one split. This block does the subtraction, and states the
agreements as flags.

It also carries the places the movement record and the flight record disagree. A record whose
aircraft type is missing, or whose filed destination differs from the movement's, is a record
that was assembled from partial information, and partial information is where the copied modes
live: every one of the 29 NM-unmatched LIRF departures of 2025 with a schedule gap over 12 h
has a null `ac_type`.

`ROW_LOCAL`: every column is a function of that row's own fields. Nothing reads a label.

Columns: `cs_eobt_is_sched`, `cs_lobt_is_sched`, `cs_iobt_is_sched`, `cs_aobt_is_sched`, `cs_any_plan_is_sched`, `cs_aobt_minus_sched`, `cs_delay_band`, `cs_ac_type_null`, `cs_ac_type_disagrees`, `cs_ades_disagrees`, `cs_rule_disagrees`, `cs_disagreements`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
TOL_PLAN: 60
TOL_AOBT: 120
DELAY_EDGES: [-1800.0, 0.0, 900.0, 3600.0, 10800.0, 43200.0]
```

### context_window

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/context_window.py`](../src/taxiout/features/context_window.py); used by 9 of the 16 configs above.

The airport's state around the takeoff, as windowed *means* rather than counts.

Our traffic blocks count movements (`congestion`, `queue`, `runway_history`) and our taxi-in block
is a static per-stand median (`taxi_in`). Team outgoing-boat's public solution measured three
windowed means that we did not have — together worth −9.1 board seconds to them (their v11), and
the idea is taken from there (https://github.com/EnioAguiar/prc-taxiout-2026). The code is ours.

All keyed on the departure's takeoff time `t` (`mvt_time`), from columns the ranking set
carries for every row:

* **neighbours' off-block proxy**: mean of `mvt_time − aobt_3` over the *other* departures with
  takeoff in `[t − W, t)` (`prev`) and `(t, t + W]` (`next`), per airport and per airport ×
  runway, W ∈ {15, 60} min. The proxy is kept only within [0, `PROXY_MAX`]. Plus the row's own
  proxy minus the 60-minute airport means — how unusual this flight's AOBT is for the moment.
* **live arrival taxi-in**: mean `taxi_sec` (clipped to [0, `TAXI_IN_MAX`]) and count of the
  arrivals landing in `(t − W, t]`, per airport and per airport × runway.
* **last arrival at the stand**: age and taxi-in of the last arrival whose in-block time is at or
  before `t` at the same airport × stand, if within a day. Keyed on the takeoff, so it can be the
  aircraft that took the stand *after* this one left — information the ranking set carries.

`CONTEXT`: other rows' times and the arrivals' own taxi times; never a departure's label.

Columns: `cw_nb_prev_apt_15`, `cw_nb_prev_apt_60`, `cw_nb_prev_rw_15`, `cw_nb_prev_rw_60`, `cw_nb_next_apt_15`, `cw_nb_next_apt_60`, `cw_nb_next_rw_15`, `cw_nb_next_rw_60`, `cw_own_minus_prev_apt_60`, `cw_own_minus_next_apt_60`, `cw_arr_tin_apt_15`, `cw_arr_tin_apt_60`, `cw_arr_tin_rw_15`, `cw_arr_tin_rw_60`, `cw_arr_n_apt_15`, `cw_arr_n_apt_60`, `cw_arr_n_rw_15`, `cw_arr_n_rw_60`, `cw_stand_last_age`, `cw_stand_last_tin`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
WINDOWS: [15, 60]
PROXY_MAX: 7200.0
TAXI_IN_MAX: 3600.0
STAND_MAX_AGE: 86400.0
```

### eurocontrol_daily

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/eurocontrol_daily.py`](../src/taxiout/features/eurocontrol_daily.py); used by 8 of the 16 configs above.

EUROCONTROL's daily series per airport: regulation, slot adherence, pre-departure delay.

Team outgoing-boat joined three public EUROCONTROL CSVs per airport × UTC day (bundled with other
changes, −7.5 board to them; https://github.com/EnioAguiar/prc-taxiout-2026). The code is ours; the
files come from `scripts/pull_eurocontrol.py` into `data/external/eurocontrol/`.

Per airport × UTC day of the takeoff:

* `ec_dep_n`: departures; `ec_reg_frac`: share ATFM-regulated; `ec_reg_n`;
* `ec_late_frac` / `ec_early_frac`: share of regulated departures off-slot late / early;
* `ec_pre_min`: all pre-departure delay per IFR departure (minutes);
* `ec_atc_min`: ATC pre-departure delay per departure (minutes).

These are day-level aggregates the provider publishes from operational data, including the day
being predicted; the rules allow open, documented data and nothing restricts its timing
(outgoing-boat's reading of the rules). `CONTEXT`: external, never a row's label. **The cache key
does not see the CSV files**: rebuild with `--overwrite` if they change.

Columns: `ec_dep_n`, `ec_reg_n`, `ec_reg_frac`, `ec_late_frac`, `ec_early_frac`, `ec_pre_min`, `ec_atc_min`.

### flight_match

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/flight_match.py`](../src/taxiout/features/flight_match.py); used by 16 of the 16 configs above.

Whether the movement matched a Network Manager flight record.

Roughly 1% of movements have no NM match, and every `_flt` column is null together for them.
That looks like a nuisance and is actually a strong signal: 33 of the 34 departures in 2025 with
a taxi-out over twelve hours are unmatched rows.

The effect is **airport-specific in sign**, so it has to be used as an interaction rather than a
main effect. At LIRF unmatched departures average 6,534 s against 1,145 s for matched ones, with
29.5% exceeding two hours; at EHAM they average 600 s against 788 s, in the other direction.

This reads only the presence of `flight_id`, never a label, so it is ROW_LOCAL.

Columns: `flt_no_match`, `cat_airport_match`.

### gate_retention

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/gate_retention.py`](../src/taxiout/features/gate_retention.py); used by 8 of the 16 configs above.

Gate retention at the moment this flight pushed: who was being held, who was already moving.

Our queue blocks (`queue`, `queue2`) count aircraft between an estimated off-block and takeoff.
Team outgoing-boat added counts read at this flight's own push clock (`aobt_3`), including
the departures that were *overdue* — past their EOBT and not yet pushed — and the recent delay to
push (https://github.com/EnioAguiar/prc-taxiout-2026; −0.71 board to them). The code is ours.

At `t = aobt_3` of the row, over the other departures `j` of the same airport (or runway):

* `gr_overdue_{apt,rw}`: #{j : eobt_1_j ≤ t < aobt_3_j} — held past their EOBT at this moment.
  Only `j` with `0 ≤ aobt_3 − eobt_1 < 7200` and `mvt ≥ aobt_3` count (their guards).
* `gr_active_rw`: #{j ≠ row : aobt_3_j ≤ t < mvt_j} on the same runway — pushed, not yet airborne.
* `gr_delay_15m`: mean `aobt_3 − sched_time` of the airport's departures that pushed in
  `[t − 15 min, t)`.

Null where the row has no `aobt_3`. `CONTEXT`: other rows' timestamps, never a label.

Columns: `gr_overdue_apt`, `gr_overdue_rw`, `gr_active_rw`, `gr_delay_15m`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
{HOLD_MAX: 7200.0, DELAY_WINDOW: 15m}
```

### modes

*target_dependent*, [`src/taxiout/features/modes.py`](../src/taxiout/features/modes.py); used by 14 of the 16 configs above.

Per-cell rates of the block_time recording modes — the first target-dependent block.

On roughly 39% of 2025 departures `block_time` is the A-CDM actual off-block, and on those
rows `ob_aobt_sec` *is* the taxi: the bare identity scores RMSE 70 where the model scores 145,
because the model hedges against the rows where the recording took something else. The model
cannot un-hedge on its own — whether a row is in
the A mode is a fact about `block_time`, which the ranking set withholds.

What *can* travel is the rate. Which mode gets recorded is strongly patterned by airport, by how
late the push was, and by whether the plan times collapse onto the schedule — and those
covariates are present on every 2026 row. So this block estimates, per cell of admissible
covariates, the probability that a row's `block_time` is the A-CDM actual (`md_p_a`) and the
probability it is the schedule (`md_p_s`), and hands the model those rates.

**Why this is TARGET_DEPENDENT.** A training row's mode is computed from its `block_time`,
reconstructed as `mvt_time − taxi_sec`. Knowing `block_time` is knowing the label. So the
rates must be estimated per fold from that fold's training months only — a globally cached
version would leak every validation month's labels into its own features. This is the first real
user of the per-fold path in
`cv.build_matrix`; `tests/test_pipeline.py` carries a leak test that corrupts the held-out
labels and asserts these columns do not move.

Columns: `md_p_a`, `md_p_s`, `md_cell_n`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
TOL_SAME: 60
TOL_AOBT: 120
SHRINK_K: 200.0
DELAY_EDGES: [-1800.0, 0.0, 900.0, 3600.0, 10800.0, 43200.0]
CELL_KEY: [airport, md_delay_band, md_eobt_is_sched, md_aobt_missing]
```

### modes5

*target_dependent*, [`src/taxiout/features/modes5.py`](../src/taxiout/features/modes5.py); used by 6 of the 16 configs above.

A *trained* six-way classifier for which stamp `block_time` copies.

The successor to an earlier block (`modes4`, not in this repository), which chased the same
target with per-cell rates and failed for a reason a review pinned down precisely: rates over 406
cells never identify a source confidently — maximum `p_eobt` of **0.26**, minimum `p_none` of
**0.30**, and 41% of cells holding fewer than 50 rows against a shrinkage constant of 200. The
mixture stays permanently hedged and collapses toward the cell mean. **The concept was intact; the
instrument was not.** Dropping the two-way `modes` block cost only **+0.22**, so the bar is low
and the headroom is nearly all unrealised.

Why the headroom is worth another attempt: the label is `mvt_time − block_time` and `block_time`
is the **only** column the ranking set withholds for a departure, so wherever it is a copy of a
stamp we hold, the label is *exactly knowable*. The source distribution over 2,062,623 matched
2025 departures at `|block_time − stamp| <= 60 s`: none 67.0%, `aobt_3` 21.0%, `eobt_1`
9.8%, `lobt` 1.7%, `sched_time` 0.5%, `iobt` 0.05%. With the source known perfectly, a
CatBoost member's trimmed ex-LIRF goes 220.94 -> **203.36**: −17.58, larger than the entire
feature programme to that date.

**Three changes over `modes4`, each from the review rather than from taste.**

1. **A trained classifier, not a cell table.** An `LGBMClassifier` for the binary
   copy/non-copy question reaches leave-one-month-out AUC 0.863, far more than a cell table over
   the same covariates could.
2. **Signed inter-stamp gaps, not agreement bits.** `modes4` reduced `eobt_1 − aobt_3` to one
   bit at a 60 s threshold. The magnitude and sign of that gap is almost certainly what decides
   which stamp got recorded, and a boolean discards it. This block feeds all ten signed pairwise
   gaps plus each stamp's gap to takeoff.
3. **Median, not mean, for the "none" fallback.** `modes4` used the mean of a right-skewed
   distribution and consequently over-predicted by a consistent **+68 to +72 s** on held-out rows.

**And one the review did not ask for, which matters more than any of them.** A classifier's
in-sample predictions are *sharp* where shrunk cell rates are blunt, so using them directly on the
training rows would hand the downstream model a column that is far more accurate in training than it
can ever be in validation — and the model would learn to trust it accordingly. `modes` gets away
with in-sample cell rates because shrinkage keeps them blunt. A classifier does not. So the training
rows here get **internally cross-fitted** predictions: the training months are split into three
groups, each group predicted by a classifier fitted on the other two. Rows outside the training
months get a classifier fitted on all of them. That is four fits per fold and it is not optional.

**Why TARGET_DEPENDENT.** The class label is computed from `block_time`, reconstructed as
`mvt_time − taxi_sec`. Knowing `block_time` is knowing the label, so everything here is fitted
per fold from that fold's training months only. `tests/test_pipeline.py` leak-tests every
target-dependent block by corrupting held-out labels and asserting the columns do not move.

**Cost warning for that leak test.** It computes the block twice over the full spine, so for this
block it is **eight classifier fits** and roughly 2.5 GB, so run the suite on a machine with room
for it. It is also why `CLF_PARAMS` must be deterministic:
the test compares the two computes column by column.

Columns: `m5_p_aobt`, `m5_p_eobt`, `m5_p_lobt`, `m5_p_iobt`, `m5_p_sched`, `m5_p_none`, `m5_p_copy`, `m5_top_prob`, `m5_label_mix`, `m5_label_copy`, `m5_entropy`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
SOURCES: [aobt_3, eobt_1, lobt, iobt, sched_time]
TOL: {aobt_3: 120.0, eobt_1: 60.0, lobt: 60.0, iobt: 60.0, sched_time: 60.0}
CLASSES: [aobt_3, eobt_1, lobt, iobt, sched_time, none]
N_INNER: 3
CLF_PARAMS: {objective: multiclass, num_class: 6, n_estimators: 150, num_leaves: 31, learning_rate: 0.15,
  min_child_samples: 200, subsample: 0.8, subsample_freq: 1, colsample_bytree: 0.8, reg_lambda: 1.0, random_state: 0,
  deterministic: true, force_row_wise: true, n_jobs: 8, verbose: -1}
PAIRS:
- [aobt_3, eobt_1]
- [aobt_3, lobt]
- [aobt_3, iobt]
- [aobt_3, sched_time]
- [eobt_1, lobt]
- [eobt_1, iobt]
- [eobt_1, sched_time]
- [lobt, iobt]
- [lobt, sched_time]
- [iobt, sched_time]
NUMERIC: [t_aobt_3, t_eobt_1, t_lobt, t_iobt, t_sched_time, g_aobt_3_eobt_1, g_aobt_3_lobt, g_aobt_3_iobt,
  g_aobt_3_sched_time, g_eobt_1_lobt, g_eobt_1_iobt, g_eobt_1_sched_time, g_lobt_iobt, g_lobt_sched_time,
  g_iobt_sched_time, n_null_stamps, utc_hour, dow]
CATEGORICAL: [airport_code, operator_code]
FEATURES: [t_aobt_3, t_eobt_1, t_lobt, t_iobt, t_sched_time, g_aobt_3_eobt_1, g_aobt_3_lobt, g_aobt_3_iobt,
  g_aobt_3_sched_time, g_eobt_1_lobt, g_eobt_1_iobt, g_eobt_1_sched_time, g_lobt_iobt, g_lobt_sched_time,
  g_iobt_sched_time, n_null_stamps, utc_hour, dow, airport_code, operator_code]
```

### modes6

*target_dependent*, [`src/taxiout/features/modes6.py`](../src/taxiout/features/modes6.py); used by 4 of the 16 configs above.

The `block_time` source classifier, decomposed into two stages.

What limits :mod:`taxiout.features.modes5` is not capacity. On the 190,713 held-out July rows the
six-way classifier recalls `none` 78% of the time, `aobt_3` 49%, and **`eobt_1` 8.5%** — the
second commonest `block_time` source is nearly invisible to it. One softmax over six classes
where `none` holds 54% of the rows spends its capacity separating the two big classes. Three
remedies: class weights, balanced subsampling, or a two-stage decomposition. This block is the
third, with the first folded in.

**Stage 1 — copy or not.** A binary classifier on every training row: does `block_time` copy any
stamp? The binary question is the one `modes5` already answers reasonably, and a binary
`LGBMClassifier` reaches leave-one-month-out AUC 0.863 on a near relative of it.

**Stage 2 — which stamp, among copies only.** A five-way classifier fitted **only on copy rows**,
where the imbalance is 71,804 / 11,420 / 2,505 / 1,142 / 96 rather than 103,746 against everything.
Two versions are fitted:

- *calibrated* (unweighted): its conditional `p(s | copy)` times stage 1's `p(copy)` gives joint
  probabilities that are still probabilities, so the label mixture stays an expectation. These are
  the `m6_p_*` columns and everything derived from them.
- *balanced* (class weights `n / (K · n_c)`, sklearn's "balanced"): its posterior trades
  calibration for recall on the minority stamps, which is exactly what `modes5` lacks. These are
  the `m6_pb_*` columns and `m6_label_copy_b`. They are emitted beside the calibrated ones,
  never mixed into them, because a reweighted posterior is not a probability of the true class.

**Everything else is `modes5`'s,** and deliberately so, because every piece of it was a fix for a
measured defect: the per-stamp match tolerance, signed inter-stamp gaps, the median rather than the
mean for the "none" fallback (+68 to +72 s over-prediction in an earlier version), zero mass on a
null stamp, copy-conditional entropy (see `modes5`), and **internal cross-fitting** — the
training months are split into three groups, each predicted by classifiers fitted on the other two,
so the downstream model never sees sharper-than-honest probabilities on its own training rows.
Classifier capacity is `modes5`'s too, so a change in the result is attributable to the
decomposition and not to more trees.

Those helpers are duplicated from `modes5` rather than imported: a block's cache key hashes only its
own defining module, so an import would let an edit there fail to invalidate this block.

**Why TARGET_DEPENDENT.** The class label is computed from `block_time`, reconstructed as
`mvt_time − taxi_sec`. Everything is fitted per fold from that fold's training months only;
`tests/test_pipeline.py` leak-tests it along with every other target-dependent block.

**Cost.** Three classifiers × four fits per fold = twelve, against `modes5`'s four. Stage 2 fits on
the ~46% of rows that copy a stamp. The leak test computes the block twice, so run the suite on a
machine with room for it (we used 31 GB).

Columns: `m6_p_aobt`, `m6_p_eobt`, `m6_p_lobt`, `m6_p_iobt`, `m6_p_sched`, `m6_p_none`, `m6_p_copy`, `m6_top_prob`, `m6_label_mix`, `m6_label_copy`, `m6_entropy`, `m6_pb_aobt`, `m6_pb_eobt`, `m6_pb_lobt`, `m6_pb_iobt`, `m6_pb_sched`, `m6_label_copy_b`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
SOURCES: [aobt_3, eobt_1, lobt, iobt, sched_time]
TOL: {aobt_3: 120.0, eobt_1: 60.0, lobt: 60.0, iobt: 60.0, sched_time: 60.0}
NONE: 5
N_INNER: 3
STAGE1_PARAMS: {objective: binary, n_estimators: 150, num_leaves: 31, learning_rate: 0.15, min_child_samples: 200,
  subsample: 0.8, subsample_freq: 1, colsample_bytree: 0.8, reg_lambda: 1.0, random_state: 0, deterministic: true,
  force_row_wise: true, n_jobs: 8, verbose: -1}
STAGE2_PARAMS: {objective: multiclass, num_class: 5, n_estimators: 150, num_leaves: 31, learning_rate: 0.15,
  min_child_samples: 200, subsample: 0.8, subsample_freq: 1, colsample_bytree: 0.8, reg_lambda: 1.0, random_state: 0,
  deterministic: true, force_row_wise: true, n_jobs: 8, verbose: -1}
PAIRS:
- [aobt_3, eobt_1]
- [aobt_3, lobt]
- [aobt_3, iobt]
- [aobt_3, sched_time]
- [eobt_1, lobt]
- [eobt_1, iobt]
- [eobt_1, sched_time]
- [lobt, iobt]
- [lobt, sched_time]
- [iobt, sched_time]
NUMERIC: [t_aobt_3, t_eobt_1, t_lobt, t_iobt, t_sched_time, g_aobt_3_eobt_1, g_aobt_3_lobt, g_aobt_3_iobt,
  g_aobt_3_sched_time, g_eobt_1_lobt, g_eobt_1_iobt, g_eobt_1_sched_time, g_lobt_iobt, g_lobt_sched_time,
  g_iobt_sched_time, n_null_stamps, utc_hour, dow]
CATEGORICAL: [airport_code, operator_code]
FEATURES: [t_aobt_3, t_eobt_1, t_lobt, t_iobt, t_sched_time, g_aobt_3_eobt_1, g_aobt_3_lobt, g_aobt_3_iobt,
  g_aobt_3_sched_time, g_eobt_1_lobt, g_eobt_1_iobt, g_eobt_1_sched_time, g_lobt_iobt, g_lobt_sched_time,
  g_iobt_sched_time, n_null_stamps, utc_hour, dow, airport_code, operator_code]
```

### offblock

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/offblock.py`](../src/taxiout/features/offblock.py); used by 16 of the 16 configs above.

Off-block time proxies.

The target is `mvt_time - block_time`, and `block_time` is what the ranking set removes.
But the dataset keeps four *other* estimates of when the aircraft left the stand, and the gap
between takeoff and each of them is a direct estimate of taxi-out.

`aobt_3` is by far the best of them, with one caveat:
where Eurocontrol never observed the off-block it back-computed the value by subtracting a
fixed default taxi time from the takeoff, leaving spikes at 20, 25 and 12 minutes. Measured
against a local baseline those account for ~12-13% of departures.

The flags emitted here mark **a band containing excess default mass, not a fabricated row** —
most of the 12-minute band is genuine traffic that happens to taxi for twelve minutes. A model
is expected to learn "trust the value less here", which is the honest reading.

Columns: `ob_aobt_sec`, `ob_aobt_is_default_12min`, `ob_aobt_is_default_20min`, `ob_aobt_is_default_25min`, `ob_aobt_is_missing`, `ob_eobt_sec`, `ob_lobt_sec`, `ob_iobt_sec`, `ob_sched_sec`, `ob_aobt_minus_eobt`, `ob_aobt_minus_lobt`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
DEFAULT_BANDS:
  ob_aobt_is_default_12min: [690, 750]
  ob_aobt_is_default_20min: [1170, 1230]
  ob_aobt_is_default_25min: [1470, 1530]
```

### opdi

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/opdi.py`](../src/taxiout/features/opdi.py); used by 1 of the 16 configs above.

Same-aircraft ground time from the OPDI flight list (EUROCONTROL PRC + OpenSky, v002).

Team likable-eagle (repository OpenAir) joined the OPDI flight list to departures by callsign and
took the aircraft's previous leg: `icao_turn = first_seen − previous last_seen`. On LIRF
NM-unmatched rows a long turn (≥ 2 h: the aircraft sat at the airport) went with a normal taxi
(median 1,132 s) behind a large gate delay, and short turns with `T ≈ D` (schedule copies). Their
board moved −0.48 with it as a feature of the gate-delay model (v23) and −1.37 with a long-hold pull
(v24) (https://github.com/ChandanHegde07/OpenAir). The files come from `scripts/pull_opdi.py`; the
organiser accepted OPDI as open data.

**Matching.** Candidate callsigns, tried in order: the NM callsign; the movement's flight number;
the flight number with a doubled airline prefix removed (`ITYTY672` → `ITY672`, `RYRR8830`
→ `RYR8830`, `QFAQFA6` → `QFA6`), a form many 2026 rows use. A departure takes the OPDI
flight with that callsign whose `adep` is its airport and whose `first_seen` — lift-off, not
off-block (likable-eagle's E46: median MVT − first_seen −26 s at LIRF) — is nearest its take-off,
within `TOL` seconds.

**Outputs.** `op_found` is 1 when a flight matched, else 0. The rest are null where unmatched:
`op_turn_s` = first_seen − the same icao24's previous `last_seen`, kept inside `TURN`;
`op_same_apt` = 1 when that previous leg ended at this airport; `op_lag_s` = first_seen −
take-off (match quality).

`CONTEXT`: external data; never a departure's label. **The cache key does not see the files**:
rebuild with `--overwrite` after a pull.

Columns: `op_found`, `op_turn_s`, `op_same_apt`, `op_lag_s`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
TOL: 1800.0
TURN: [1200.0, 129600.0]
KEYS: [k_nm, k_raw, k_dedup]
```

### queue2

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/queue2.py`](../src/taxiout/features/queue2.py); used by 2 of the 16 configs above.

Queue depth with the estimated off-block taken from the flight plan first.

The same sweep as :mod:`taxiout.features.queue`, with one parameter changed: the estimated
off-block coalesces `eobt_1` before `aobt_3`. An external review rebuilt the blinded
analysis's `q_ahead` observably and found the plan-first ordering worth 5.6 s of held-out
group-mean RMSE over the actual-first one (398.6 against 404.2, baseline 413.9), which is the
opposite of what :mod:`queue` assumes. Kept as its own module so `f23_queue` stays
reproducible — the feature cache is keyed on module source.

Original rationale follows.

Queue depth on the tarmac — how many aircraft are taxiing around me, not how many took off.

Every existing congestion column is anchored on `mvt_time` and counts *takeoffs* in a
trailing window, which measures throughput. What a taxiing aircraft actually waits behind is
queue **depth**: the number of other aircraft that pushed back before it and have not yet
left the ground. The blinded analysis measured this as the strongest dynamic driver available
(correlation with clean taxi 0.40 at EGLL, 0.39 LTFM, 0.34 LFPG; airport x q_ahead reaches
held-out RMSE 390.3 against 413.9 for airport alone — `scripts/analysis/fresh_fable/
f03_congestion.py`), and dismissed it as unusable because it needs other flights'
`block_time`. It does not: an *estimated* off-block from the flight-plan columns is enough,
and those are present on every 2026 row.

Computed as a sweep. Each departure contributes +1 at its estimated off-block and −1 at its
takeoff; the running sum over an airport is the number of aircraft on the move at any instant.
Reading that curve at my own off-block gives the queue ahead of me, and at my takeoff the
queue behind. `CONTEXT`, not target-dependent: no label is touched — `aobt_3`, `eobt_1`,
`iobt`, `lobt` and `sched_time` are all available for 2026 departures.

Columns: `q2_ahead_at_ob`, `q2_still_at_tko`, `q2_ahead_rw`, `q2_est_ob_source`, `q2_est_taxi_sec`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
OB_SOURCES: [eobt_1, aobt_3, iobt, lobt, sched_time]
```

### runway_config

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/runway_config.py`](../src/taxiout/features/runway_config.py); used by 16 of the 16 configs above.

Which runways the airfield is actually using, around the moment of takeoff.

A stand's distance to the runway is fixed; the runway it is sent to is not. Reconfiguration
turned out to be the largest single driver we have found — it produced the worst day of Rome's
2025 (13 July, +8.52) and a 2.54x swing in Amsterdam's arrival taxi-in *inside the scored month*,
where departing 36L gives 234-332 s and departing 24 gives 545-657 s.

Everything here is built from `runway` and `mvt_time`, both of which the ranking set keeps,
and it uses arrivals as well as departures because arrival rows are intact there too. No labels
are read, so this is `CONTEXT`: computed once over both sets, no fold-aware handling.

The unit is the airport-hour. Finer buckets would resolve a mid-hour switch but would also make
the smaller airports' shares noisy — LSZH averages about fifteen departures an hour.

Columns: `rwy_cfg_code`, `rwy_dep_active_n`, `rwy_arr_active_n`, `rwy_share_in_hour`, `rwy_is_dominant`, `rwy_shared_with_arrivals`, `rwy_cfg_changed`, `rwy_cfg_seen_n`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
{MIN_SHARE: 0.05, BUCKET: 1h}
```

### runway_history

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/runway_history.py`](../src/taxiout/features/runway_history.py); used by 14 of the 16 configs above.

The runway's own day: who went before, what wake they carried, how the day is flowing.

Community intel made concrete: separation minima make the *pair* of wake categories on a
runway the physical unit of queue spacing (a 241 s gap is congestion for a medium behind a
medium and pure physics for a light behind a super), and the runway's day-so-far tells the
model whether it is living a quiet morning or a pressured evening.

Whole-day statistics are used deliberately. The organisers state the model is **post-operational,
not tactical** — hindsight within the day is licensed — and every input here is a `mvt_time` or
`runway` field, all present in the ranking set. `CONTEXT`: other rows, never a label.

Columns: `rh_prev_wake`, `rh_pair`, `rh_gap_vs_pair`, `rh_day_seq`, `rh_day_n_rw`, `rh_day_median_gap`, `rh_next15m_rw`.

### schedule

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/schedule.py`](../src/taxiout/features/schedule.py); used by 2 of the 16 configs above.

The airline schedule, and what it means when nothing else is known.

`sched_time` is the only time reference that survives on the rows that decide the metric.
Departures with no Network Manager match are 1.6% of rows and 57.6% of the squared error, and
every `_flt` column is null together for them — `aobt_3` and `eobt_1`, the two strongest
features in the model, are absent for exactly those rows. `sched_time` is a movement-record
field and is present on 100% of them.

The gap between takeoff and schedule behaves completely differently on each side of that flag.
Over 2025, a gap above twelve hours means a mean taxi of 1,262 s and P(taxi > 12 h) = 0.0018
when the flight matched; when it did not, the same gap means a mean of 26,978 s and
P(taxi > 12 h) = 0.387, over 75 rows. Inside the unmatched population the gap correlates 0.442
with the target overall and 0.896 at LIRF, against 0.205 on matched rows.

`sc_gap_nomatch` exists because of how trees reach that cell. Given the gap and the flag
separately, the model needs two splits to isolate a region holding 22 rows of the seasonal folds,
which its leaf constraint forbids. Carrying the
interaction as its own column turns that into one split on a value no matched row can hold.

Everything here reads the row's own fields, so it is `ROW_LOCAL`. `mvt_time` is the takeoff
time, which is given in the ranking set; only `block_time` is blanked.

Columns: `sc_gap_sec`, `sc_gap_nomatch`, `sc_has_sched`, `sc_sched_hour`.

### snow

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/snow.py`](../src/taxiout/features/snow.py); used by 5 of the 16 configs above.

Snow at the departure airport: how much, for how long, and how recently.

`weather` carries the latest METAR's snow flag, which says nothing about a storm's size or about
the day after it. In February 2025 Istanbul's taxi-outs ran 15–16 minutes long on its snow days,
and still 3 minutes long on the freezing day after, and the models missed most of it
(`scripts/analysis/a127_february_error.py`). Here, from the same METAR reports, at the takeoff
time `t`:

* `sn_3h` … `sn_48h`: snow reports (SN, SG, PL, GS) in the preceding window;
* `sn_heavy_6h`: heavy snow (+SN) reports in the last 6 h; `fz_6h`: freezing rain or drizzle;
* `sn_day`: snow reports over the whole UTC day of the takeoff (post-operational: the organisers
  frame the task as such, and the day's weather is known after the day);
* `sn_last_h`: hours since the last snow report, capped at 96;
* `sn_48h_cold`: snow in the last 48 h and the latest temperature at or below 0 °C.

CONTEXT: METAR only, no labels.

Columns: `sn_3h`, `sn_6h`, `sn_12h`, `sn_24h`, `sn_48h`, `sn_heavy_6h`, `fz_6h`, `sn_day`, `sn_last_h`, `sn_48h_cold`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
WINDOWS_H: [3, 6, 12, 24, 48]
LAST_CAP_H: 96.0
```

### stand_geometry

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/stand_geometry.py`](../src/taxiout/features/stand_geometry.py); used by 14 of the 16 configs above.

Stand-to-threshold distance from the X-Plane Scenery Gateway packs.

The stand term of the location backbone is largely geometry (correlation up to 0.895 at
LIRF-25, weighted mean 0.597), and geometry generalises to stands the training data never
saw — EDDM's July-2026 apron is 7.9% unseen stands. Distance joins on the normalized
stand key; rows without coordinates (LTFM entirely, parts of EDDM/LSZH) keep a null distance
plus an explicit flag, which gives tree models the clearly separate bucket.

Columns: `sg_dist_thr_m`, `sg_has_geo`.

### stand_runway

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/stand_runway.py`](../src/taxiout/features/stand_runway.py); used by 10 of the 16 configs above.

Categorical identity of the movement: where it started, where it left from, what it was.

Emitted as integer codes against a vocabulary built once from every movement in the spine,
training and ranking together. Building the vocabulary globally is what makes the codes stable
across folds; it involves no labels, so it leaks nothing.

Columns: `cat_airport`, `cat_stand`, `cat_runway`, `cat_ades`, `cat_ac_type`, `cat_wake`, `cat_operator`, `cat_market_segment`, `cat_flight_type`, `cat_flight_rule`, `cat_stand_runway`, `cat_airport_runway`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
CATEGORICALS: {airport: cat_airport, stand: cat_stand, runway: cat_runway, ades: cat_ades, ac_type: cat_ac_type,
  wake_cat: cat_wake, operator: cat_operator, market_segment: cat_market_segment, flight_type: cat_flight_type,
  flight_rule: cat_flight_rule}
```

### stand_runway_lo

*row_local*, [`src/taxiout/features/stand_runway_lo.py`](../src/taxiout/features/stand_runway_lo.py); used by 6 of the 16 configs above.

The low-cardinality half of `stand_runway` — a direct response to the ablation.

`s02_drop_stand_runway` scored trimmed ex-LIRF **223.48** against the champion's **225.99**, on a
config identical except for that one block: **dropping all twelve categorical codes improves the
model by 2.51**, which is larger than the training-label cap's 2.36 and second only to the CatBoost
function class (−6.29). Removing features is not supposed to help by that much.

The cardinalities say why:

======================  =============
column                  levels (2025)
======================  =============
`cat_stand_runway`          12,053
`cat_stand`                  1,900
`cat_ades`                   1,569
`cat_operator`                 677
`cat_ac_type`                  270
`cat_airport_runway`            70
`cat_runway`                    53
`cat_airport`                   10
======================  =============

They are handed to LightGBM as `categorical_feature`, and LightGBM partitions a categorical by
sorting its levels on gradient statistics and cutting — which overfits badly at 12,053 levels
against `min_data_in_leaf=100`. This converges with two other findings: XGBoost's weakness was
its categorical handling (it earned an NNLS weight of 0.0000 in the stack), and CatBoost's
*strength* is its ordered target statistics on exactly these columns (−6.29 in CV).

So the question the ablation cannot answer is whether the block is harmful *as a whole* or only in
its high-cardinality half. This block keeps the codes at or below `MAX_LEVELS` and drops the rest,
which is the smallest change that separates those two readings.

Deliberately a separate module rather than a parameter on `stand_runway`: the cache key is a hash
of the whole defining module, so editing that file would invalidate the block every shipping member
uses and force a full rebuild.

Columns: `lo_airport`, `lo_runway`, `lo_wake`, `lo_market_segment`, `lo_flight_type`, `lo_flight_rule`, `lo_airport_runway`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
CATEGORICALS: {airport: cat_airport, stand: cat_stand, runway: cat_runway, ades: cat_ades, ac_type: cat_ac_type,
  wake_cat: cat_wake, operator: cat_operator, market_segment: cat_market_segment, flight_type: cat_flight_type,
  flight_rule: cat_flight_rule}
MAX_LEVELS: 100
KEEP: [airport, runway, wake_cat, market_segment, flight_type, flight_rule]
```

### taxi_in

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/taxi_in.py`](../src/taxiout/features/taxi_in.py); used by 16 of the 16 configs above.

Taxi-in statistics as a proxy for the *unimpeded* part of taxi-out.

An arrival taxiing from runway to stand covers much the same ground a departure covers in
reverse, and arrivals barely queue — so the median taxi-in at a stand is close to a measurement
of how far that stand is from the runways, uncontaminated by departure queueing.

Two things make this worth having. It is not target-dependent: it reads `taxi_sec` on *arrival*
rows, which are fully present in the ranking set, so it needs no fold-aware treatment and can be
computed contemporaneously for 2026 rather than carried over from 2025. And the residual it
leaves behind — taxi-out minus this — isolates pushback and queueing, which is the part actually
worth modelling.

It is not a drop-in substitute for taxi-out, and the airport interaction is not optional. Where
arrivals and departures share runways it tracks well (EHAM 0.84 at stand level, LEMD 0.78); where
they are segregated it does not (LEBL −0.09, which runs zero shared runways), and at queue-bound
Heathrow stand-to-stand variation is drowned by the queue (0.09).

Columns: `ti_stand_median`, `ti_stand_n`, `ti_stand_runway_median`, `ti_stand_runway_n`, `ti_airport_median`, `ti_stand_vs_airport`.

Settings (the module's constants):

```yaml
PLAUSIBLE_TAXI_SEC: [60, 7200]
MIN_OBSERVATIONS: 20
```

### weather

*context*, [`src/taxiout/features/weather.py`](../src/taxiout/features/weather.py); used by 14 of the 16 configs above.

Weather at the departure airport, anchored on takeoff time.

Open METAR from the IEM archive (`scripts/pull_metar.py`). Everything here is backward-looking
from `mvt_time`: the latest observation, short rolling precipitation windows, freezing hours,
and the run of consecutive sub-zero days ending yesterday — the de-icing memory that a single
observation misses. Post-ops licensing would even allow forward windows, but the January story
this block chases (de-icing, snow banks, LVP) is carried by what already happened.

Columns: `wx_temp_c`, `wx_dew_spread_c`, `wx_rh`, `wx_wind_kt`, `wx_gust_kt`, `wx_wind_dir_sin`, `wx_wind_dir_cos`, `wx_vis_km`, `wx_precip_mm`, `wx_precip_3h_mm`, `wx_precip_6h_mm`, `wx_snow`, `wx_freezing`, `wx_fog`, `wx_ts`, `wx_frozen_hours_24h`, `wx_deice_proxy`, `wx_subzero_streak_days`, `wx_obs_age_s`.
